title: Farmers Market

jokes.text: Leslie compliments Ben's slacks in a professional city manager meeting, escalating into mutual declarations of love while Ron sits silently furious
jokes.setup: Leslie is presenting a report to Ben as city manager in an official capacity
jokes.punchline: The professional meeting devolves into Leslie and Ben complimenting each other, declaring love, and trying to include Ron — who just wants them to stamp a form
jokes.explanation: Works beautifully because it's rooted in character — Leslie and Ben being professionally married is a natural absurd extension of who they are. The escalation from 'nice slacks' to 'I'm in love with you' is perfectly paced. Ron's mounting fury and ultimate physical response is the real punchline. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, that tie really brings out your eyes. Have you been working out? Those shirts fit you differently.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben reveal they rehearsed finishing each other's sentences — naked in bed
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben finish each other's sentences in perfect sync, suggesting an adorable couple moment
jokes.punchline: Ben adds 'Naked in bed' — revealing they literally rehearsed this at home, undercutting the romantic spontaneity
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely sharp joke. The misdirection works on two levels: the cute 'we finish each other's sentences' bit is revealed to be rehearsed (already funny), and then Ben casually adds the nakedness. The economy is excellent — two words do enormous work. Highly quotable and perfectly in character for Ben's deadpan delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I was just being friendly. Calling Leslie 'adorable' is a term of endearment, it doesn't have to be inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Ben, she works for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I call Tom 'buddy' all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you're not trying to sleep with me.

jokes.text: 'I think our love made him angry' / 'I think he broke my wrist. I'm not kidding.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben insist on including Ron in a group hug despite his obvious displeasure
jokes.punchline: Ron apparently crushes someone's wrist during the forced group hug, reported with casual matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: Ron's physicality is perfectly in character — his iron grip as an involuntary expression of contained rage is a great visual gag inferred from dialogue. 'I think he broke my wrist' delivered as an afterthought is strong deadpan. The 'I'm not kidding' adds a beat of sincerity that makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We finish each other's sentences.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's like we share the same—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Brain.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Exactly. And we're so comfortable with each other that we practice conversations naked in bed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we rehearse what we're gonna say to people before we say it to them.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Completely nude. For hours sometimes.

jokes.text: Ann: 'I'm a crazy shape. This morning when I got out of bed, I just tipped forward like a poorly made bowling pin.'
jokes.setup: Ann is heavily pregnant and responding to Leslie's cheerful check-in
jokes.punchline: The 'poorly made bowling pin' simile is specific, visual, and self-deprecating in a way that lands perfectly
jokes.explanation: The bowling pin simile is an unexpectedly specific and vivid image that elevates what could have been a generic pregnancy complaint. 'Poorly made' is the key modifier — it implies the design flaw, not just the weight. Good economy and a strong, quotable image.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What did we just—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We told them everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Everything.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Except that I'm a whale and that my feet already kill.' Chris: 'Whales don't have feet.'
jokes.setup: Ann uses 'I'm a whale' as a hyperbolic complaint about her pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Chris takes it completely literally, correcting the zoological inaccuracy rather than engaging with her emotional complaint
jokes.explanation: Five words of punchline, and they land cleanly. Chris's literal-mindedness is perfectly in character and the economy is excellent. The joke also does double duty by establishing the Chris/Ann dynamic that the whole B-plot hinges on.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I need to tell you something. I love you. I'm in love with you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we're in a public meeting right now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't care. Everyone needs to know that you're the best thing that's ever happened to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I love you too, but this is highly inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Inappropriate? This is the most appropriate thing I've ever done!

jokes.text: Cut from Ann describing Chris as 'wonderful and thoughtful and positive' directly to Ann in talking head: 'He's driving me up the fucking wall.'
jokes.setup: Ann (or Chris) warmly describes Chris as wonderful and thoughtful in voiceover
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to Ann's talking head confessional: 'He's driving me up the fucking wall' — the rare Parks and Rec f-bomb making it land harder
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest structural comedy moment. The juxtaposition cut is perfectly executed — the setup is the warm praise, the punchline is the immediate contradiction. The f-bomb is almost never used in Parks and Rec, which makes it a genuine surprise and amplifies the impact enormously. Maximum economy: two scenes, one line, huge laugh. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what any of you are talking about. I'm going to my office to do some woodworking.

jokes.text: Chris cheerfully calls out 'Smoothie's ready!' immediately after Ann's 'driving me up the wall' confession
jokes.setup: Ann has just vented about Chris being infuriatingly helpful and positive
jokes.punchline: Chris's oblivious cheerful smoothie announcement confirms everything Ann just said, in real time
jokes.explanation: Three words do massive work. The joke is entirely structural — Chris's obliviousness is the joke, and hearing him shout cheerfully RIGHT after Ann's vent is perfect comic timing built into the edit. A great example of mockumentary form being used as comedy delivery system.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, Ron! Group hug!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would rather die.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: GH! GH everyone!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What does GH mean?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Group hug! It's faster!

jokes.text: Leslie at the farmers market: 'Look at this tiny tree. Can you eat this? Aww. This one's dead.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving a proud speech about the farmers market she created as city councilor
jokes.punchline: She immediately gets distracted by bonsai-sized produce, poking it with innocent curiosity, then noting one is dead
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie — pivoting from earnest civic pride to childlike curiosity without missing a beat. 'This one's dead' delivered flatly after 'Aww' is a good small gag. Character-specific and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, come here, group hug!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Come on, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm warning you people.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Three, two, one!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I tried to warn you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ow, ow, ow! Ron, your belt buckle is stabbing me!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And you're stepping on my foot!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I said no.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Hey, Connie Cabbage.' / Connie: 'Green cabbage is always a safe bet. Red cabbage is good. I mean, you can't go wrong. That's the fun thing about cabbage.' / Leslie: 'One of the fun things.'
jokes.setup: Leslie greets a cabbage vendor at the market with enthusiastic familiarity
jokes.punchline: Connie delivers a deeply earnest and unironic defense of cabbage; Leslie's 'One of the fun things' suggests she has thought more deeply about cabbage fun than this conversation covers
jokes.explanation: A small gem. Connie's sincere cabbage enthusiasm is absurd, and Leslie's correction ('One of the fun things') implies she has a richer taxonomy of cabbage fun than this conversation allows. Both characters are played completely straight, which is the right call.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I feel like a whale. My feet are killing me.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, whales don't have feet. They have flippers. So anatomically, you're more of a manatee.

jokes.text: The Chardbodies stand banners: 'Chardbodies: Get a chard on' and 'Let's get re-charded in here!'
jokes.setup: A new vendor has set up at the farmers market with dancers and party energy
jokes.punchline: The signage reveals their branding is built entirely on chard-based sexual innuendo puns
jokes.explanation: 'Get a chard on' is a genuinely good pun — the double meaning is immediate and the commitment to the bit (entire branding built around it) amplifies it. 'Re-charded' is slightly weaker but the escalation works. Pun-writing quality is actually high here.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm so clumsy right now. I feel like a bowling pin that was made on a Friday afternoon by someone who didn't care anymore.

jokes.text: Shirtless Chardbodies dancers selling vegetables like it's a nightclub, offering 'chard shots' and 'chard poppers'
jokes.setup: A standard farmers market setting
jokes.punchline: The Chardbodies operation is a fully realized strip-club-meets-vegetable-stand concept with shots, poppers, and dancers
jokes.explanation: The commitment to the absurd premise makes this work. The escalation from sexy chard stand to chard shots for 'freaky vegans' is perfectly calibrated Pawnee lunacy. Visual comedy that requires no explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I could rub your feet. I've taken a prenatal foot massage course.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You took a prenatal foot massage course?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, I watched a video on BabyCenter.com about it. Apparently, if you press the wrong spot on a pregnant woman's foot, it can induce labor.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's not real.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Are you sure? Because I'm not taking any chances.

jokes.text: Leslie's farmers market signs: 'Peas be kind to others,' 'In case of fire, romaine calm,' 'You won't bay leaf how nice olive our vendors are'
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Leslie has actual written rules of conduct; she references 'the wooden sign'
jokes.punchline: Three escalating vegetable puns on official signage — each one more elaborate than the last, culminating in 'bay leaf/olive' as a multi-pun sentence
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Leslie-specific comedy. The escalation from one pun to three, culminating in a sentence that packs in two vegetable puns ('bay leaf' + 'olive') on an official government sign, is perfectly absurd. The character integration is outstanding — only Leslie would make official safety signage this way. Highly quotable. The talking head confession 'I don't like vegetables, but I'm very good at vegetable puns' is the perfect punctuation.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris is really great. He's so positive and energetic, and he cares so much about the work. I think he's an amazing guy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: But my God, he is exhausting. Like, relentlessly so. I feel like I need a nap after every conversation with him.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'I don't like vegetables, but I'm very good at vegetable puns.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just rattled off three elaborate vegetable puns
jokes.punchline: She confesses she doesn't even like vegetables — the puns are entirely disconnected from any actual appreciation for the subject matter
jokes.explanation: This one-liner is nearly perfect. It retroactively recontextualizes the puns as a pure skill divorced from any content affinity — a very Leslie Knope thing. The economy is exceptional: ten words that are instantly quotable and deeply character-specific. One of the episode's best individual lines.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at all these vegetables! Are these... are these locally sourced?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Yes, everything here is grown within ten miles.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's amazing. Do you grow these indoors or outdoors? Actually, don't answer that. I'm going to guess... both?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Outdoors.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, because that's where the sun is. I knew that. How much for the... the leafy greens? Are those vegetables or just leaves you picked up?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Those are lettuces.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Of course they are. I'm going to buy all of them and have them for dinner tonight. Raw. Like nature intended.

jokes.text: April is sitting on Andy's lap while he plays guitar and sings an improvised song about needing to use the bathroom
jokes.setup: April is sitting on Andy's lap
jokes.punchline: Andy is singing a spontaneous song about needing to poop while April is on his lap, with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Very Andy — his complete lack of social filter means he's narrating his bodily needs in song form in mixed company. The absurdity is character-driven but the joke itself is fairly simple lowbrow humor.

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: You like cabbage? Because let me tell you, there are SO many fun things about cabbage!

dialogue.speaker: Connie
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.line: Well... it's round. And it's... also green.

jokes.text: April: 'Okay, I'm gonna need the sarcasm to take a long walk right now.'
jokes.setup: Andy has called his guitar 'a super small piano'
jokes.punchline: April dismisses his quip with a hilariously deadpan command for sarcasm to leave — but Andy wasn't being sarcastic at all
jokes.explanation: April's response is funny in its own right as a phraseable dismissal, and funnier still because she misreads Andy's sincerity as sarcasm. The gap between her interpretation and Andy's genuine belief adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Nolan
dialogue.line: Welcome to Sexy Chard! Get your sexy chard here!

dialogue.speaker: Nolan
dialogue.line: This chard is so hot, it needs a cold shower!

dialogue.speaker: Nolan
dialogue.line: Come get your greens, baby! This chard will make you blush!

jokes.text: Tom in talking head: 'Split that four ways, boom. $600.'
jokes.setup: $150 has been agreed as the fee for Mouse Rat
jokes.punchline: Tom confidently announces the math: $150 divided by 4 equals $600, delivered with the swagger of someone who definitely did the math
jokes.explanation: Tom's math is confidently, catastrophically wrong, delivered with total conviction. The 'boom' is the key word — his swagger makes the failure funnier. Very Tom-specific character comedy.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'I'll say it again: The men's room needs a separate dispenser for face wash. I can't wash my face with hand soap. Look at these pores. They're gaping.'
jokes.setup: Tom is in the whine & cheese club monthly complaint session
jokes.punchline: Tom's workplace complaint is entirely about skincare — his pores, specifically — and the urgent need for face wash separate from hand soap
jokes.explanation: Deeply Tom Haverford. His workplace grievances are entirely aesthetic — this is not what the HR process is designed for. 'They're gaping' delivered with genuine distress is perfect. The 'I'll say it again' implies this is a repeat complaint, adding character depth.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Oh wow, this is... this is just regular chard. This isn't sexy at all. It tastes like chard. It's bitter and earthy and honestly kind of disappointing.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'The rules do not specify whether or not I'm allowed to listen to Willie Nelson on my headphones.'
jokes.setup: Ron is legally required to hold a monthly HR session for employees to air grievances
jokes.punchline: Ron has found the loophole: technically nothing says he has to listen. Willie Nelson headphones on.
jokes.explanation: This is elite Ron Swanson comedy. The joke perfectly encapsulates his philosophy: fulfill the letter of any bureaucratic requirement while actively subverting its spirit. 'The rules do not specify' is a Ron Swanson sentence. Willie Nelson specifically is perfect. Highly quotable and rewatch-worthy. Approaches the 8.0 anchor and clears it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: These vendors are completely violating the rules!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What rules? What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My rules! I made them very clear.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, those are just vegetable puns on a wooden sign.

jokes.text: While Kyle complains about his parking spot being taken, Ron hums along to Willie Nelson with headphones on
jokes.setup: Kyle is complaining about someone parking in his spot — the fourth time this month
jokes.punchline: Ron is visibly not listening, humming along to his music while Kyle pours his heart out
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of Ron humming along while Kyle suffers is the delivery mechanism for the earlier talking head joke. Works well as a callback visual gag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what, Ben? I'm not going to apologize for my vegetable puns. In fact, I think they're radishing. Absolutely radishing. And if you don't like them, you can turnip the heat in here because I'm on a roll. A whole wheat roll. With vegetables in it.

jokes.text: Donna: 'I just want to choke him until he passes out.' — delivered as a workplace HR complaint about Kyle
jokes.setup: Donna is next in the rotation to complain about workplace grievances
jokes.punchline: Her grievance about Kyle parking in her spot is delivered as a desire to commit light strangulation
jokes.explanation: Donna's contained fury delivered as matter-of-fact desire for mild violence is a reliable character beat. The specificity of 'until he passes out' (not 'to death') somehow makes it funnier — she just wants him unconscious.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have created an elaborate system of vegetable puns and rules that I follow religiously.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I have to be honest with you... I don't even like vegetables.

jokes.text: Ann's whine & cheese spiral: 'I want to be Pac-Man, and instead of dots, I want 'em to be cinnamon buns.'
jokes.setup: Ann has ceded Donna's complaint time to vent about her pregnancy food restrictions and cravings
jokes.punchline: A steadily escalating list of forbidden foods — pork rinds, jelly beans, trash bag of mashed potatoes — culminates in Ann wanting to become Pac-Man eating rows of cinnamon buns
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest moments. The escalation from reasonable cravings to 'trash bag of mashed potatoes' to 'I want to be Pac-Man' is a masterclass in comedic escalation. Each step is bigger than the last, and the Pac-Man image is so specifically odd and vivid that it becomes instantly quotable. The follow-up line 'I want to be a giant head and a mouth' doubling down seals it.

dialogue.speaker: Connie
dialogue.line: If you want to compete with the sexy chard stand, you're gonna have to sex up your vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean, sex them up?

dialogue.speaker: Connie
dialogue.line: Well, look at the cabbage guy over there. He's really putting himself out there.

jokes.text: Ann continues: 'I want to be a giant head and a mouth, and I just want to eat rows and rows of junk food pellets, and where's my trash bag of potatoes?'
jokes.setup: Ann has already described wanting to be Pac-Man eating cinnamon buns
jokes.punchline: She expands the Pac-Man fantasy further — 'giant head and a mouth' — then snaps to demanding the trash bag of potatoes in the room, as if someone should have fetched it
jokes.explanation: The callback to the trash bag of potatoes while simultaneously expanding the Pac-Man bit shows the rant has internal logic. 'Where's my trash bag of potatoes?' as a sincere in-room demand is perfectly unhinged. This and the previous joke form one escalating sequence — both score high.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He plays ukulele. There's a difference.

jokes.text: 'Porn on the cob.' / 'I'm sorry. I'm just very good at that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie argues that the Chardbodies stand constitutes vegetable porn
jokes.punchline: She immediately generates 'Porn on the cob' as a pun, then steps back to self-admiringly note her aptitude
jokes.explanation: The callback to Leslie's pun-making skill is earned, and 'porn on the cob' is actually a good pun. Her self-congratulatory meta-comment perfectly mirrors the earlier talking head confession. The joke is self-aware in the best way.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So how much do you want to charge for the kids' party?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know, like fifty bucks?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fifty dollars? That seems reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, or did you mean fifty cents? Because I would also do it for fifty cents.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that's a quarter per hour.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know what I said.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Time.' then 'Yikes.' after Ann's rant
jokes.setup: Ann has delivered a passionate, escalating rant about pregnancy cravings and wanting to be Pac-Man
jokes.punchline: Tom's one-word timer-call followed by 'Yikes' is the perfect understated response to the emotional intensity
jokes.explanation: The two-word reaction does real work — 'Yikes' is the only correct response and Tom delivering it clinically is funny. Good economy, modest originality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so we made $500 from that gig. There's five of us in the band, so that's... $500 divided by five... carry the one... $8,000 each!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, that doesn't seem right. Let me recalculate. $500 times five equals... negative $2,000. So we each owe $2,000.

jokes.text: Leslie arrives at Ben's car in the parking lot with a binder and argues that the parking lot is city hall property, defeating the firewall
jokes.setup: Ben established a 'firewall' rule that they only discuss work at city hall
jokes.punchline: Leslie has immediately found a jurisdictional loophole — the parking lot is city property — so the firewall is down
jokes.explanation: Leslie's immediate exploitation of the loophole is perfect Leslie Knope — she agreed to the rules and spent the next hour finding the exceptions. The jurisdictional argument is played completely straight, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My pores are like the Grand Canyon. You could land a helicopter in there. I'm pretty sure there's a Native American tribe living in my left cheek.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals an entire new farmers market rule book she 'stayed up all night' writing, plus toffee surprises as a bribe
jokes.setup: Ben needs a legitimate reason to revoke the Chardbodies' license
jokes.punchline: Leslie has overnight produced a 158-page rule book specifically designed to target Chardbodies, plus handmade toffee surprise candies as a reward for compliance
jokes.explanation: The toffee surprise detail is the key addition — it's not just that she made rules, she also made artisanal candy as an incentive. 'The surprise is there's toffee in the inside' is funny in its literal explanation of the surprise. This is quintessential Leslie: overwhelming effort, good intentions, slightly inappropriate execution.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What are you guys doing?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whine and cheese.

jokes.text: 'Leslie's toffee surprise. The surprise is there's toffee in the inside.'
jokes.setup: Leslie pulls out handmade toffee as a bribe for Ben to revoke the license
jokes.punchline: She explains the 'surprise' — it is toffee. That is the surprise. She named it this.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan anti-reveal ('the surprise is... toffee') is a compact, clean joke. Leslie's earnest explanation of what 'surprise' means in this context is funny because she clearly doesn't register that it undermines the name.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant, so I have to pee all the time. It's like there's a violent beach ball inside me that's constantly pushing down on my bladder.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Good day, colleague.' — formal greeting to his wife after the firewall conversation
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie agreed to treat each other professionally at work
jokes.punchline: Ben greets Leslie with robotic professional formality — 'Good day, colleague' — as a straight-faced attempt to honor the firewall
jokes.explanation: Economy is nearly perfect — three words that are inherently funny by being so wrong for the relationship. Ben's deadpan commitment to an absurd posture is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I can't eat soft cheese! I can't eat deli meat! I can't eat sushi! I can't even have caffeine! Do you know what I can eat? Nothing! I can eat nothing!

jokes.text: Chris's nipple kit speech: 'nipple cream, nipple pads, and also a special nipple pimple ointment in case you develop any pimples on your nipples.'
jokes.setup: Chris is trying to be the perfect supportive partner and has been researching Ann's pregnancy needs
jokes.punchline: He launches into an extremely detailed, clinical nipple speech with the phrase 'nipple pimple' as the crescendo, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The escalating repetition of 'nipple' is a classic comedy of accumulation. Chris's sincerity is what makes it work — he's not embarrassed at all. 'Nipple pimple' as a clinical compound noun is the payoff. Ann's breaking point ('you have to stop using the word nipple') is the audience surrogate moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm like Pac-Man, just eating cinnamon buns in a maze, and the ghosts are just chasing me around, but I don't care because I'm eating cinnamon buns.

jokes.text: Emergency whine & cheese club called by Ann; Ron puts on headphones and Larry is immediately dispatched to 'get in there'
jokes.setup: Ann needs to vent and seeks out the whine & cheese club
jokes.punchline: Ron's immediate headphone protocol — established earlier — is now a running gag; Larry is used as furniture
jokes.explanation: Competent callback to the established gag. Ron's immediate compliance with his own system is funny. Larry being summoned with no explanation and following orders is good Larry comedy. Not exceptional but solid.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I just want to be Pac-Man, you know? Just moving through life, eating everything in my path, not worrying about anything else. Just eating and moving, eating and moving.

jokes.text: Ann venting about vomiting in whine & cheese club while Mouse Rat's song about 'Sex Is Cool' plays in background
jokes.setup: Ann is in the emergency whine & cheese session to vent about pregnancy symptoms
jokes.punchline: The soundtrack of the scene is Mouse Rat rehearsing 'Sex Is Cool' — a song about sex, playing over a woman describing the miseries of pregnancy (i.e., the consequence of sex)
jokes.explanation: A nice structural irony — the juxtaposition of 'Sex Is Cool' playing over pregnancy vomiting complaints is the kind of background joke that rewards attentive viewers. Functionally a visual/audio gag built into the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What reason could we possibly give to kick out the chard vendors?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Porn on the cob.

jokes.text: April booked Mouse Rat for a kids' birthday party; Andy thought it was 'a festival' where 'Dave Grohl might be there'
jokes.setup: Mouse Rat is discussing their setlist, including songs called 'Drunk Off Our Asses' and 'Sex in Space'
jokes.punchline: They realize April booked them for a six-year-old's birthday party; Andy believed Dave Grohl 'might be there'
jokes.explanation: The band's setlist names ('Sex in Space,' 'Drunk Off Our Asses') being revealed in the context of a kids' party setup is good misdirection. April's straight-faced non-explanation 'You said Dave Grohl might be there' is perfect April logic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm on a roll. A whole wheat roll.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm getting better at this pun thing.

jokes.text: April's defense: 'Dave Grohl might be there. I don't know. He might be anywhere. The guy's awesome, and he's unpredictable.'
jokes.setup: Andy is upset that April misled him about Dave Grohl attending
jokes.punchline: April's defense is philosophically airtight: she didn't say he would be there, just that he might — and he might be anywhere
jokes.explanation: April's logic is perfectly April — technically unassailable, completely disingenuous, and delivered with absolute conviction. 'He might be anywhere' as a defense is genuinely funny argumentation. The 'He's awesome, and he's unpredictable' is the perfect kicker. Highly quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We need to establish a firewall between our work and personal relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A firewall? Ben, I'm not a computer system that needs protecting.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, I mean we need boundaries. Clear separation. Like a firewall.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, did you just try to use IT jargon to describe our relationship? That's the least romantic thing you've ever said to me.

jokes.text: Andy calling after departing bandmate: 'Shaq might be there!'
jokes.setup: April's 'Dave Grohl might be there' defense; the bandmate is leaving
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately adopts April's strategy — 'Shaq might be there!' — not Dave Grohl, not anyone from music, but Shaquille O'Neal
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect callback joke. Andy sees April's technique work and immediately mimics it — but picks Shaq, a basketball player with no connection to a kids' birthday party, which somehow makes it funnier than Dave Grohl. The specificity of Shaq is inspired. The brevity (four words) is perfect. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so a nuclear explosion happens and Indiana Jones just hides in a refrigerator? A refrigerator! And somehow he survives completely unscathed? That's not how physics works! That's not how any of this works! And then—and THEN—he swings on vines with monkeys like he's Tarzan? Indiana Jones is an archaeologist, not a primate! This movie is an insult to cinema, to archaeology, and to refrigerators everywhere!

jokes.text: The new farmers market rule book targeting Chardbodies includes 'No chard-related innuendo' as a universal rule
jokes.setup: Ben reads Leslie's overnight rule book and notes it seems to target one vendor
jokes.punchline: The rules include 'No chard-related innuendo' — a rule so specific it can only apply to one entity in human history
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurd specificity — 'chard-related innuendo' is such a niche category of prohibited content that it's immediately funny. Leslie's attempt to frame it as a universal rule makes it worse (better).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying if I technically didn't know the firewall existed, I wouldn't be breaking it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, Leslie, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I'm choosing not to know about it right now.

jokes.text: Ben points out that Leslie's new 158-rule farmer's market rulebook may be 'specifically targeting chardbodies,' citing 'No visible cleavage. No strobe lights. No chard-related innuendo.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has written an extensive new rulebook ostensibly for all vendors
jokes.punchline: Ben identifies that despite Leslie's claims of universality, one of the rules is literally 'no chard-related innuendo' — obviously targeting a specific vendor
jokes.explanation: A solid procedural joke — the existence of a rule called 'no chard-related innuendo' is itself funny as a legal document item, and it exposes Leslie's transparently motivated rulemaking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I made toffee surprise!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What's the surprise?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Toffee.

jokes.text: Nolan defends chard: 'You try selling it without sexy dancers. It's impossible. It's like, hey, you like lettuce? Try this. It's worse. It tastes like kale took a dump on spinach.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Nolan to just sell something else if chard is hard to sell
jokes.punchline: Nolan's defense of his marketing approach includes a devastating chard review — 'kale took a dump on spinach'
jokes.explanation: 'Kale took a dump on spinach' is a genuinely funny food description — unexpected, vivid, and accurate to how chard actually tastes to many people. The logic of the whole speech (chard is so bad you need strippers to sell it) is absurd but internally consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I feel like my stomach is expanding in all directions. I'm like one of those old-fashioned globes that opens up to reveal a bar inside.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I like to think of it as celery with B.O.'
jokes.setup: Nolan has described chard's terrible taste
jokes.punchline: Leslie has her own chard description ready — 'celery with B.O.' — which implies she has thought about this before
jokes.explanation: Five words, strong image. 'Celery with B.O.' is a concise, vivid food metaphor that earns a genuine laugh. Leslie having this formulation ready suggests she's been thinking about this, which is also character comedy. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Okay, so nipple soreness is very common during pregnancy. You might want to try some nipple cream. I have nipple cream in my office. Would you like me to get my nipple cream? I'm very comfortable talking about nipples. Nipples, nipples, nipples.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Ben not to go home because 'if we go home, the firewall is up, and you don't have to deal with me anymore'
jokes.setup: Ben wants to leave after the Chardbodies confrontation; Leslie suspects his motives
jokes.punchline: Leslie correctly identifies that Ben's firewall idea was partly to have a zone of protection from her
jokes.explanation: Competent plot-comedy — the meta-acknowledgment that the firewall is partly about Ben managing Leslie's intensity is a good character moment but not a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, please stop saying 'nipple.' I'm begging you.

jokes.text: Donna and Ron have replaced whine & cheese club with sushi and cigar club, locking Ann out
jokes.setup: Ann has been taking over the whine & cheese club with her pregnancy complaints
jokes.punchline: Donna and Ron have mutinied — it's now sushi and cigar club. Ron: 'This is a Cuban.' / Donna: 'This is yellowtail. I feel amazing.'
jokes.explanation: The pivot from whine & cheese to sushi and cigars is a good escalation of the running gag. Ron's specific identification of his Cuban — delivered with the satisfaction of a man who earned this cigar — is great character comedy. Donna's immediate parallel is perfect. Both characters feel exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I was trying to avoid saying... that word. So I said 'boob hats' instead.

jokes.text: Ann: 'But you know what? I would yell some more, but I think I just peed my pants a little bit.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been building to an emotional confrontation about needing to vent
jokes.punchline: She deflates herself — mid-confrontational speech — with an accidental pants-wetting admission
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — Ann builds to a righteous moment then completely undercuts it with bodily betrayal. 'A little bit' as a qualifier adds the perfect touch of dignity-preservation. A good pregnancy comedy beat with strong timing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Alright guys, let's run through our setlist for the kids' party tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: One, two, three, four!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: 🎵 She took me down to the river, said 'Boy, you better learn to swim,' If you don't know how to love a woman, then you don't know... 🎵

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, those are completely inappropriate lyrics for a children's party.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? Kids love this song!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I don't think the parents are going to appreciate it.

jokes.text: Ron: 'What's happening now? Is the nurse upset?' / Ron: 'I don't care.'
jokes.setup: Ann has just made an emotional speech and peed her pants a little
jokes.punchline: Ron, still wearing headphones for most of this, checks in with minimal interest and immediately withdraws it
jokes.explanation: Ron's sequence — minimal curiosity immediately followed by 'I don't care' — is very Ron. The brevity and commitment are the joke. Not exceptional but consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Band member
dialogue.line: We're playing for kids? At a six-year-old's birthday party?

dialogue.speaker: Band member
dialogue.line: Dave Grohl is gonna be there.

jokes.text: Ben sends Larry to read a letter instead of facing Leslie himself, then is discovered sitting in his parked car right outside
jokes.setup: Ben sends Larry to deliver a message to Leslie in the conference room
jokes.punchline: Leslie finds Ben sitting in the parking lot, having used Larry as a proxy to avoid her while technically honoring the firewall
jokes.explanation: Using Larry as a messenger while hiding in the car is a perfectly Ben move — cowardly but legally precise. The physical image of Ben in the parking lot is a strong visual gag. Escalates the firewall running gag well.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, you don't know where Dave Grohl is right now. He could be anywhere. He could be in this room. Have you checked everywhere?

jokes.text: Donna to Chris: 'You've fallen into a classic trap, Christopher — trying to fix a woman's problems instead of just listening to what they are!'
jokes.setup: Chris is confused that Ann is upset with him for being too helpful
jokes.punchline: Donna explains it as a 'classic trap' with the authority of someone who has seen this many times
jokes.explanation: Competent but the joke leans on a fairly well-worn comedy premise (men trying to fix rather than listen). Donna's delivery and the 'Christopher' formality save it somewhat. Not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Band Member
dialogue.line: I'm quitting the band. This is too rabbinical for me.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Umbilical? Dude, we're not even pregnant.

jokes.text: Ron (outraged): 'Why are you yelling?' / Donna: 'Tom put all my records into this rectangle!'
jokes.setup: The serious conversation about Chris and Ann's communication problem
jokes.punchline: Ron interrupts the scene with his rectangle grievance again — mid-serious-conversation
jokes.explanation: The callback works because the timing is perfect — Ron keeps erupting about the rectangle in the middle of unrelated conversations. The repetition adds value rather than diminishing it.

dialogue.speaker: Nolan
dialogue.line: Chard needs sexy marketing. It tastes like a stripper's armpit.

jokes.text: Tom: 'What she needs from you is to just look her in the eyes, nod your head, and say those two magic words: That sucks.'
jokes.setup: Tom is advising Chris on relationships — framed as wisdom from someone who has 'read instructional books to trick women into liking him'
jokes.punchline: The two 'magic words' are 'that sucks' — the most minimal possible acknowledgment positioned as profound relationship advice
jokes.explanation: The buildup to 'those two magic words' primes the audience for something insightful, and 'that sucks' is a perfect anti-climax. Tom's framing of emotional intelligence as a 'trick' and the confession that he reads books 'to trick women into liking him' is also a good character beat. Quotable advice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chard is like if a vegetable gave up on life. It's sad lettuce. Limp, lifeless sad lettuce that tastes like dirt and broken dreams.

jokes.text: Ron erupts again: 'The songs just play one right after the other! This is an excellent rectangle!'
jokes.setup: Ron has been complaining about the rectangle throughout; now he's apparently using it
jokes.punchline: Having just condemned the rectangle, Ron is now discovering its virtues mid-conversation — it plays songs automatically
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the rectangle running gag is excellent. Ron going from outrage to wonder — 'This is an excellent rectangle!' — delivered with the same intensity as his complaints, is perfectly Ron. The running gag structure builds to this correctly, and the timing (mid-other-conversation) is ideal. One of the episode's best running gag payoffs.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: An approval pen? Leslie, that's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not? Well, I made you one anyway.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I am super chill all the time!' — delivered in the fountain, clearly not super chill
jokes.setup: Ben says arguing with Leslie is like 'arguing with the sun' — overwhelming and hot
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defensive response is to very passionately insist she is 'super chill all the time' — demonstrating the opposite
jokes.explanation: Classic ironic self-description. The joke is entirely in the delivery and context — standing in a fountain, having orchestrated an elaborate jurisdictional chase — and insisting she's 'super chill all the time' is perfectly ironic. Great character integration. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you're out of the complaining club.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because you're always so positive and optimistic. You don't fit in with us.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, what are you guys going to do instead?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We've upgraded to more luxurious vices. We're now a brandy and cigar club.

jokes.text: Ben: 'This is un-charded territory for us.'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to make a serious point about their professional relationship
jokes.punchline: He deploys a chard pun in the middle of a heartfelt speech — 'un-charded territory' — and immediately seems pleased with himself
jokes.explanation: Ben's chard pun lands exceptionally well because it comes in the middle of a sincere moment — he's doing the thing Leslie does (vegetable puns at inappropriate times) without meaning to. Leslie's appreciative 'Oh, that's nice' / 'I learned from the best' exchange makes it a genuine couple moment. Compact and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I can't believe you guys would exclude me like this! I thought we were friends! I thought—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: *suddenly clutches stomach* Oh god, the baby is kicking. Does anyone have any pickles?

jokes.text: Ben's chard pun: 'I'm your boss. This is "un-charded" territory for us.' Leslie: 'Oh, that's nice. Thanks. I learned from the best.'
jokes.setup: Ben is making a serious point about the complexity of their professional relationship
jokes.punchline: He lands an 'un-charded territory' pun mid-serious speech; Leslie immediately recognizes it, compliments it, and credits herself as his teacher
jokes.explanation: The pun is good on its own — 'uncharted/un-charded' — but the real joke is the callback structure: Ben has absorbed Leslie's vegetable pun habit, Leslie recognizes her influence, and they share a sweet comedic moment even mid-argument. 'I learned from the best' with Leslie as the best is perfect character integration. A warm, well-constructed joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Dear Leslie, you are the most beautiful, intelligent, and kind woman I have ever met. I love you more than—

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Huh. That's nice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Give me that!

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben realize they can't move because their legs are numb from the fountain
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben have just had a sincere reconciliation in the fountain
jokes.punchline: 'Let's get out of this fountain.' / 'I can't because my legs are numb.' / 'Yeah, I can't move. Are we gonna die here?'
jokes.explanation: A good physical comedy button on the fountain sequence — the sweet resolution is immediately undercut by the consequence of standing in freezing water for the length of an argument. 'Are we gonna die here?' as a genuine question is a good deadpan kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm getting out of here. I'm driving away and never coming back.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't leave. I already filed a complaint with the Department of Transportation about your vehicle registration. Your car is now flagged in the system.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? How is that even possible?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a laminated copy of every municipal code in Indiana. Also, I may have called ahead to the next three counties.

jokes.text: Larry's reaction to the fountain standoff: 'I don't like this game. I don't know what the rules are!'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are stuck in a fountain arguing about jurisdiction
jokes.punchline: Larry, observing from outside, has interpreted the entire jurisdictional standoff as some kind of game — and is upset he doesn't know the rules
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry. He's been watching the whole thing and his takeaway is that he's been excluded from a game. The genuine hurt in 'I don't know what the rules are' is very Larry Gergich. Good economy and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We made it! We're safe!

jokes.text: Andy's revised kids' song: changes 'Sex Hair' to 'Sex Bears' — 'You got sex bears, you got 'em from me, kids'
jokes.setup: Andy has been told the problem with 'Sex Hair' — the word 'hair' was not the issue
jokes.punchline: He changed 'hair' to 'bears' and presents 'Sex Bears' as the children's appropriate version
jokes.explanation: Andy's specific failure mode — changing the wrong word — is a great Andy joke. He heard the feedback ('this song is inappropriate for kids') and misidentified the problem as the word 'hair.' 'Big ol' sex bears' as a children's song lyric is wonderfully wrong. April's 'Andy, the word hair was not the problem with Sex Hair' is the perfectly timed correction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You want to keep this going? Fine. I'm going to the city council meeting tomorrow and I'm going to tell them EVERYTHING. About the fountain, about your little water sanctuary, all of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I can. And I will. Because that's what happens when you mess with me and my town.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Oh, it's sex! Oh, crap.' — genuine realization
jokes.setup: April tells Andy the word 'hair' was not the problem with Sex Hair
jokes.punchline: A genuine moment of dawning comprehension from Andy — 'Oh, it's sex! Oh, crap.' — as if this had not occurred to him
jokes.explanation: The punchline is Andy's total sincerity in his belated understanding. 'Oh, it's sex!' delivered as a discovery rather than a statement is perfectly in character. The 'oh, crap' follow-up is the right button. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is this? Some kind of rectangle?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: How do I operate it? Where do I put the records?

jokes.text: Tom: 'Have you not lost it?' in response to 'Or I am going to lose it!'
jokes.setup: Tom is screaming at Andy while threatening to 'lose it'
jokes.punchline: Andy's callback observation that Tom has already clearly lost it
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient counter — four words perfectly timed. Not particularly original but well-executed in the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is this? Some kind of music box?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Wait, you can... arrange the songs in any order you want?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen.

jokes.text: Tom's aunt describes her nephew Sebastian as 'something of an outcast' and says he's 'a horrible little tyrant'
jokes.setup: She's appealing to Andy's sympathy — this party will determine Sebastian's social status
jokes.punchline: She describes Sebastian warmly as an outcast to garner sympathy, then can't help admitting he's 'a horrible little tyrant'
jokes.explanation: The honest contradiction — pitching sympathy while accidentally revealing genuine contempt for the child — is a clean joke. 'Don't ruin this day for him!' adds a nice layer of pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't argue with Leslie because it's like arguing with the sun. You can't win. The sun is too powerful, and if you get too close, it will destroy you.

jokes.text: April introduces Andy as 'Johnny Karate and his magical guitar stick' with no preparation
jokes.setup: April needs to introduce the performer for the kids' party; Andy has no prepared persona
jokes.punchline: April invents 'Johnny Karate and his magical guitar stick' on the spot — complete fabrication delivered as if it's a real thing
jokes.explanation: 'Johnny Karate' is inspired — it has nothing to do with music or children's entertainment and everything to do with the random associations in April's head. The 'magical guitar stick' is almost redundant in its wrongness. This moment also plants the seed for the show's later 'Johnny Karate' spinoff, making it a rewatch moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're too passionate about everything.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am NOT too passionate! That is the most insulting thing anyone has ever said to me, and I have literally fought everyone in this office!

jokes.text: Andy's improvised kids' song: picking your nose and putting it on your friend, peeing the bed until age 32
jokes.setup: Andy has to perform for children without any prepared material
jokes.punchline: He improvises songs about boogers, bed-wetting until 32, and safety tips — performed with complete commitment
jokes.explanation: Andy's improvisational performance is a showcase for Chris Pratt's ability to commit fully to absurd material. The escalation from nose-picking to 'I personally peed the bed until I was 32' is Andy Dwyer's confessional comedy at its best — he's sharing himself as the lesson. The kids' delight makes it land even harder.

jokes.text: Andy's song: '♪ Everybody pees the bed / Just something that we do / I for instance peed the bed / Until I was 32'
jokes.setup: Andy is performing a children's party song about normal, relatable behaviors
jokes.punchline: He normalizes bed-wetting by casually disclosing he personally did it until age 32 — oversharing with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A standout joke. The structure is perfect: universal premise ('everybody does it') → personal confession → absurd age revelation ('until I was 32'). It's both a good children's song parody and a great character revelation. The song format makes the oversharing hit harder. One of the episode's best moments — Andy's innocence makes it sweet rather than disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait. Wait wait wait. Ben, do you realize what this means?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're stuck. We're actually stuck in this fountain.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We're not stuck, Leslie. We can just walk out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Ben. We're stuck. Emotionally. Spiritually. This fountain has claimed us.

jokes.text: Andy becomes 'Bert Macklin' mid-performance, the FBI agent who investigates stinky feet, then launches into the 'Stinky Feet Patrol' song
jokes.setup: Andy's performance has been going well with nose and bathroom humor
jokes.punchline: He spontaneously breaks into his Bert Macklin FBI agent persona, redirecting it into a children's song about stinky feet — improvised worldbuilding in real time
jokes.explanation: Bert Macklin is an established Andy persona from earlier seasons; bringing it into the children's performance is a great character callback. The FBI agent who investigates stinky feet is a perfect child-appropriate adaptation of the bit.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Everyone, this is Andy Dwyer, also known as DJ Roomba.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He spins records and cleans up messes.

jokes.text: Tom's aunt: 'I cannot believe this only cost me 150 bucks.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just delivered a spectacular (to children) performance as Johnny Karate
jokes.punchline: Tom's aunt's reaction underscores the absurd cost-to-value ratio — Mouse Rat is incredibly cheap and apparently incredible for 6-year-olds
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the birthday party subplot. The callback to the $150 fee works because the performance has been so entertainingly unhinged. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ♪ There's a booger in my nose, and it's green, it's green! The biggest booger that you've ever seen! ♪

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ♪ I could flick it, I could pick it, I could roll it in a ball, I could stick it on my shirt or on the wall! ♪

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ♪ Booger, booger, booger, booger, booger on my toe! Booger, booger, booger, booger, now it's in my hello! ♪

jokes.text: Ann tells Chris about her leg pain: 'It's like I have a tension headache, but in my calves.'
jokes.setup: Chris has been coached to just say 'that sucks' and listen; Ann describes her symptoms
jokes.punchline: The 'tension headache but in my calves' is a weirdly specific and accurate description that's funny in its earnestness
jokes.explanation: A quirky but specific complaint that earns a small laugh from its oddness. Works better as setup for the 'that sucks' callback payoff than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: When you're a kid, there's so many things that happen to everyone, you know? Universal experiences that bring us all together.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Like, uh, wetting the bed. I wet the bed until I was twelve. No, wait—fourteen. Actually, sophomore year of high school, so... sixteen?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My mom had to use a special waterproof mattress cover. We went through like eight sets of sheets a week.

jokes.text: Ann: 'And I'm so gassy. There's just been, like, a long, slow fart stream coming out of me since we started talking... this morning.'
jokes.setup: Chris is dutifully listening and saying 'that sucks' to everything Ann says
jokes.punchline: Ann escalates to describing a sustained, ongoing flatulence situation — 'since we started talking... this morning' — with a beat before 'this morning' for maximum impact
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'this morning' is the structural key — it implies it started earlier in their conversation, then extends the timeline dramatically. Ann's matter-of-fact delivery of this information is consistent with the pregnancy venting arc and escalates the 'that sucks' callback payoff nicely.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have to say, I'm genuinely enjoying this. Tickets were only $3.

jokes.text: Chris's 'that sucks' / 'that really sucks' call-and-response with Ann's complaints
jokes.setup: Tom advised Chris that 'that sucks' are the two magic relationship words
jokes.punchline: Chris deploys the phrase with his characteristic positive intensity — 'That sucks' / 'That really sucks' — to each of Ann's complaints, with evident effort
jokes.explanation: The payoff on Tom's advice works because Chris delivers 'that sucks' with the same positive energy he uses for everything — it sounds like a compliment. 'That really sucks' as an upgrade shows Chris treating this like a skill to master. The Ann/Chris relationship resolution is well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I've been so gassy lately. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk and just... (makes continuous farting sounds) ...for like ten minutes straight. It's like my body is a broken kazoo that only plays one note.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, that's... that's a lot of information.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I know! And the smell? It could clear out a small village. I'm genuinely worried I'm going to gas out the entire office.

jokes.text: After the birthday party, a parent approaches Andy: 'My son wants you to sing at his birthday party next weekend.' April immediately: 'He is, but it's actually $250 for short notice. You can call this number and ask for April Karate.'
jokes.setup: Andy is basking in post-performance glow, uncertain about his future
jokes.punchline: April has already rebranded, inflated the price, and created a business identity ('April Karate') in the time it took the parent to finish their sentence
jokes.explanation: April taking over booking as 'April Karate' is a perfect character moment — she's entrepreneurial in the most April way possible. The price jump from $150 to $250 'for short notice' and the creation of an entire business identity is very funny and very in character. The callback to Johnny Karate makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm just so stressed about work and my apartment and everything feels like it's falling apart.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That sounds really hard.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, it is. You know what? I feel so much better. Thank you for listening.

jokes.text: Nolan's farmers market after dark opens at exactly 5:00 PM; Ben: 'Well, if this is the way people want to buy their produce, so be it.' / 'This town is full of lunatics.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben made peace with Nolan, agreeing not to revoke his license 'for now'
jokes.punchline: Nolan immediately opens Farmers Market After Dark the moment the regular market closes — and it's apparently popular
jokes.explanation: Ben's resigned acceptance is a good character button — the city manager learning to live with Pawnee's lunacy. 'This town is full of lunatics' works as an episodic closer for the Chardbodies storyline. Not exceptional but solid.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm not even going to ask. This is Pawnee. At this point, I've just accepted that there's a nighttime sexy vegetable market, and I'm okay with that.

jokes.text: Final tag: Leslie and Ben try the chard and both react with disgust. Leslie: 'It's like a tree barfed in my mouth.'
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been about Chardbodies and chard; Leslie and Ben have defended/attacked/debated it
jokes.punchline: They try chard and it's terrible — 'tree barfed in my mouth' — confirming everything Nolan said about it being disgusting
jokes.explanation: 'Tree barfed in my mouth' is a vivid, quotable food description. The episodic button works because it confirms Nolan's entire thesis about chard being awful, and Leslie's visceral metaphor is characteristic. Good closer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, what is this? It tastes like a dirty sock filled with regret.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I think I just felt my taste buds file for divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why would anyone eat this voluntarily?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I genuinely think the chard is punishing us for something we did.

tmdb_overview: On Ann and Chris's last night in Pawnee, Leslie throws a grand farewell party and attempts to fulfill one last promise. Meanwhile, Tom, Ben, Ron and Andy struggle to find the perfect going away gift for Chris.
insight: Observational humor drives a modest 78.5-score hour built on character consistency over big laughs.
